title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
question: Where do autoregressive transformers store factual associations, and can one mid-layer MLP be edited to change a single fact?
mechanism: Causal tracing: corrupt the subject tokens with noise, then restore single hidden states from the clean run; mid-layer MLP outputs at the last subject token carry the decisive effect. ROME edits one MLP projection W at layer l*: k* is the subject key at the last subject token, v* is optimized so the layer outputs the new object, and the update is closed form, W_new = W + Lambda (C^-1 k*)^T with Lambda = (v* - W k*) / ((C^-1 k*)^T k*), where C = K K^T is the uncentered key covariance pre-cached from a Wikipedia sample (Eq. 2, Sec. 3.1).
training: No network training. Each edit optimizes only the target value vector v* (Fig. 4 caption: 'value v* is optimized'). C is estimated once from a sample of Wikipedia text (Appendix E.5; sample size not extracted). The paper states the method edits a single fact at a time.
setup: GPT-2 XL on zsRE (10,000 records; compared against FT, FT+L, KE, KE-zsRE, MEND, MEND-zsRE) and on the authors' CounterFact dataset of counterfactual assertions.
numbers: Table 1, zsRE on GPT-2 XL: ROME Efficacy 99.8 (+/-0.0), Paraphrase 88.1 (+/-0.5), Specificity 24.2 (+/-0.5); unedited GPT-2 XL Efficacy 22.2 (+/-0.5).
Sec. 3.4 human evaluation: evaluators are '1.8 times more likely to rate ROME as more consistent with the inserted fact' and rate ROME '1.3 times less likely to be more fluent than the FT+L model'.
limits: Edits are directional: 'The iconic landmark in Seattle is the Space Needle' is stored separately from the reverse statement, so both need two edits (Sec. 5).
Edits one fact at a time and is 'not intended as a practical method for large-scale model training' (Sec. 5).
Human evaluators rated ROME text as somewhat less fluent than FT+L (Sec. 3.4).
Logical, spatial and numerical knowledge were not investigated (Sec. 5).
evidence_quote: In a convolutional network, Bau et al. solve this using an optimization, but in a fully-connected layer, we can derive a closed form solution:

novelty_note.A: Closed-form rank-one update of one MLP projection computed from key and value vectors taken from forward passes, but applied to a single fact rather than a behaviour.
novelty_note.C: The pre-cached covariance inverse C^-1 sets the update direction (C^-1 k*); it is not used as a gate or steering direction.

title: On the Limitations of Rank-One Model Editing in Answering Multi-hop Questions
question: Does editing one fact with ROME support multi-hop reasoning, and does spreading the same edit over several layers help?
mechanism: Redundant Editing: run ROME independently at several MLP layers (the 5th to 20th, e.g. layers 5, 8, 11, 15, 17, 20) and load all edited MLP layers into one model, so the same fact is stored at several depths. Each per-layer edit uses ROME's rank-one update, which Sec. 3.2 writes as Delta W = (k_s^T k_s)^-1 k_s^T (v_o* - W k_s), with k_s the subject activation and v_o* the desired output, both taken from forward passes. Layer combinations are chosen by sweeping, and the paper stops at 6 layers because COUNTERFACT language metrics start to fail.
training: No gradient training of the model is described. The paper inherits ROME's editing procedure and does not restate how v_o* is obtained.
setup: GPT-J-6B; MQuAKE 2-hop questions (2HQ) with single-hop edits; COUNTERFACT for specificity and naturalness metrics.
numbers: Abstract: 'improve accuracy on 2-hop questions by at least 15.5 percentage points, representing a 96% increase over the previous single-edit strategy'.
Sec. 5 (configuration 5,8,11,15,17,20): 'a 15.5 percentage point (96.3%) multi-hop accuracy gain compared to the vanilla single edit strategy'.
limits: Trades off specificity and language naturalness on COUNTERFACT; configurations beyond 6 layers show clear failures (Table 3 caption).
Overfitting: when hop-1 is edited, models sometimes prefer the edited hop-1 answer over the correct 2HQ answer (overfitting analysis, Table 4).
Analysis does not extend to other editors (fine-tuning, representation editing), other architectures, 3+ hop questions, or simultaneous multi-hop edits (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Redundant Editing strategy: insert copies of a same approach designed to edit both shallow and deep MLP

title: Unified Concept Editing in Diffusion Models
question: Can one closed-form edit of text-to-image cross-attention weights erase, debias and moderate many concepts at once without degrading unrelated generation?
mechanism: UCE updates the key and value projections W of cross-attention layers. With edit concepts c_i mapped to target vectors v_i* and preserved concepts c_j kept at W_old c_j, the closed form (Eq. 7) is W = (sum_i v_i* c_i^T + sum_j W_old c_j c_j^T)(sum_i c_i c_i^T + sum_j c_j c_j^T)^-1. The paper says this generalizes TIME and MEMIT. Debiasing (Alg. 1) keeps one vector per attribute value, adjusts its magnitude alpha <- eta (R_curr - R_des) on each iteration, and moves a concept to the preserve set once its ratio is within 0.05 of the desired ratio.
training: None: the paper states the edit is a closed-form solution and 'edits the model without training'. Debiasing uses an iterative loop over alpha that re-measures generated-image ratios (Alg. 1) rather than gradient training.
setup: Stable Diffusion cross-attention weights; erasure of up to 100 artist styles, debiasing of 35 Winobias professions, and nudity moderation on I2P prompts; COCO-30k for fidelity; Winobias and I2P for bias and safety metrics.
numbers: Joint-debiasing paragraph: 'a gender ratio deviation of 0.27 versus 0.22 for the gender-debiasing model and 0.67 for the original Stable Diffusion'.
Table 1 caption: 'Our method can erase upto 100 concepts while performing similar to pre-trained SD on COCO-30k dataset.'
limits: Removing over 500 artists degrades general image generation even with preservation terms (Discussion, before the Conclusion): the authors say 'a critical mass of artists is needed'.
Intro reports that in prior work debiasing one concept affects others; the authors claim their procedure eliminates this mutual effect.
interp: word-level composition effects, e.g. 'successful person' becoming 88% male of 100, are an example the paper gives of biases that per-attribute edits may not cover.
evidence_quote: Our method adopts that concept-erasure approach, and we benchmark against the previous state-of-the-art.

novelty_note.A: A low-rank closed-form edit of existing cross-attention weights, computed from text-encoder embeddings, that changes a behaviour (erasure, debiasing, moderation) rather than a single fact.
novelty_note.E: Reports an empirical capacity limit: erasing more than about 500 artists degrades general generation even with preservation terms.

title: LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
question: Is there a closed-form, minimal-distortion way to make a representation linearly unable to predict a concept, and can it be applied at every layer of a language model?
mechanism: Theorem 4.2: with W = (Sigma_XX)^(+1/2) (the whitening transform) and Sigma_XZ the cross-covariance, the minimal-distortion affine erasure is P* = I - W^+ P_{W Sigma_XZ} W, where P_{W Sigma_XZ} = (W Sigma_XZ)(W Sigma_XZ)^+ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of W Sigma_XZ, and the bias is b* = E[X] - P* E[X]. Concept scrubbing (Alg. 1) fits (P, b) on the hidden states at each layer, applies x -> P(x - mu) + mu, and passes the edited states to the next layer.
training: None gradient-based: the paper says LEACE 'does not require gradient-based optimization' and needs only covariance statistics, which can be computed in a streaming fashion. Scrubbing caches hidden states for training (up to 500GB in the authors' runs); recomputing them instead raises compute from O(l) to O(l^2) (Sec. 6.1).
setup: Pythia 160M to 12B and LLaMA 7B to 30B, erasing part-of-speech information from the input of each transformer block (Pile and RedPajama samples); BERT embeddings for gender bias in profession prediction.
numbers: Sec. 5: LEACE 'is around 2 orders of magnitude faster' than RLACE and does not require gradient-based optimization.
Sec. 5 (BERT): 'profession-prediction accuracy of 77.3% on the projected embeddings (compared with 79.3% over the original embeddings)'.
limits: Only linear concept erasure is studied; the authors 'conjecture that it is intractable to nondestructively edit X' against a general nonlinear adversary (Sec. 7).
Scrubbing caches hidden states for training (up to 500GB in the authors' runs); recomputing them instead raises compute from O(l) to O(l^2) (Sec. 6.1).
SAL, the full-rank baseline, causes larger perplexity increases than LEACE (Table 1).
evidence_quote: Instead, we would like to erase all linear information about a concept in the activations at every layer, which we term concept scrubbing.

novelty_note.C: Uses the whitening transform (Sigma_XX)^(+1/2) and a cross-covariance projection to remove a concept; it is an erasure of a feature rather than a gate or steering vector.

title: Controlling Language and Diffusion Models by Transporting Activations
question: Can inference-time activation steering match the optimal-transport map between source and target activation distributions, preserving those distributions, and control LLMs and diffusion models?
mechanism: Linear-ACT: for each activation coordinate, a univariate affine map T(a) = omega a + beta fitted from sorted samples A and B of source and target activations, with omega = sum_i a~(i) b~(i) / sum_i (b~(i))^2 and beta = m_b - omega m_a (Def. 3.1, using recentred sorted values). Strength lambda interpolates (1 - lambda) a + lambda T(a); lambda = 1 is full transport. A transport support limits maps to in-distribution activations. Mean-ACT and several prior steering vectors are shown to be special cases (Sec. 3.3, Table 1).
training: None gradient-based: the map is 'recovered in closed form' from sorted sample values (Def. 3.1). The sample size for each experiment is not extracted from the text read.
inference_cost: Reported as no computational overhead at inference time, because the map can be composed with the adjacent linear layer (Sec. 3.1, Appendix A).
setup: Gemma2-2B and Llama3-8B on RealToxicityPrompts (1000 prompts; toxicity, perplexity on 20k Wikipedia sentences, MMLU) and on TruthfulQA; SDXL and FLUX for style control and concept negation.
numbers: Sec. 4 (toxicity, Table 2): Linear-ACT achieves 'up to 7.5x reduction in toxicity on Gemma2-2B and 4.3x on Llama3-8B' with minimal impact on PPL and MMLU.
Sec. 4 (TruthfulQA, Table 3): 'increases MC1 by roughly 5% for Gemma2-2B and by almost 8% for Llama3-8B' at lambda = 1.
limits: No limitations section for Linear-ACT was found in the read text; Table 2 shows a small PPL increase and MMLU drop in some settings (e.g. MMLU 51.3 (-1.8) for Post-LN).
interp: per-coordinate univariate maps do not model correlations between activation dimensions (a reading of Def. 3.1, not a stated limitation).
evidence_quote: We propose Activation Transport (AC T), a framework to steer activations according to the optimal transport (OT) map between two different

title: AROMA: Autonomous Rank-one Matrix Adaptation
question: Can LoRA rank be grown automatically, layer by layer, to use far fewer parameters than fixed-rank LoRA or AdaLoRA?
mechanism: Dual-loop rank-one growth: each module starts at rank zero and adds one rank-one LoRA component at a time. The inner loop trains the current rank-one component (Delta W = sum_i B_i A_i) until an inner convergence criterion is met; the outer loop adds components until an outer criterion stops growth. Optimizer states are reset between components to keep subspaces independent (Sec. 4, Fig. 2).
training: Gradient-based fine-tuning with Adam: RoBERTa-base on GLUE, and LLaMA3-8B on commonsense170K. Automatic termination in the MRPC example occurs at 1600 to 2400 steps (Fig. 1 caption).
setup: RoBERTa-base on GLUE tasks compared with full fine-tuning, BitFit, adapters, LoRA r=1/8/16 and AdaLoRA; LLaMA3-8B on commonsense170K evaluated on ARC, OBQA, SIQA, PIQA, BoolQ and others.
numbers: Intro: AROMA uses '<10% of the parameters required by LoRA r=8 and AdaLoRA r=8 without prespecified rank'.
GLUE table (RoBERTa-base): LoRA r=8 1.34M parameters, average 85.43; full fine-tuning 125.0M parameters, average 85.40.
limits: Not yet tested in multimodal applications, and scalability to LLMs above 100B parameters is not validated (Limitations section).
Uses gradient-based training, so it does not reduce the training cost that closed-form methods target.
evidence_quote: Workflow of AROMA. For each module, AROMA trains rank-one matrices sequentially with a dual-loop architecture.

title: Keys to Robust Edits: from Theoretical Insights to Practical Advances
question: Why do locate-and-edit methods fail robustness tests (paraphrased or shuffled subjects, long context), and can disentangled keys fix this?
mechanism: Analysis: a fact's key (the MLP input used by ROME-style editors) is compared in a whitened space; the paper shows that keys for rephrased or shuffled subjects diverge, and that unrelated entities overlap (key collisions). REP (Robust Edit Pathway) adds an adapter to the key: k_hat = f_gate(k) * f_proj(k) + k (Eq. 3). The projection is trained with an aggregation loss that pulls same-subject keys toward the target key k* under the C^-1 whitened inner product (Eq. 4), plus a consistency loss (Eq. 6, L = L_agg + alpha L_consistency). At test time a token-level gate threshold tau decides whether the projection is applied.
training: Gradient-trained adapter (projection and gate) on keys of the same subject; the paper states REP 'requires additional training steps to learn the adapter parameters'. Training sizes are not extracted.
inference_cost: Not quantified; the authors state REP adds computational overhead compared to direct editing methods (Sec. 9).
setup: ROME, MEMIT, R-ROME and EMMET on LLaMA2-7B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2-7B, using CounterFact and ZsRE; robustness tests of paraphrased subjects, shuffled subject tokens and long context.
numbers: Abstract: REP 'improves success rate over robustness tests by up-to 66.4% while maintaining the success rate unaffected'.
Table 1 (EMMET row) contains the entry '82.7+66.4'; the abstract attributes the up-to 66.4-point gain to REP on robustness tests.
limits: Single-fact editing only; interrelated or continual edits are left open (Sec. 9).
Requires additional training of the adapter, adding overhead (Sec. 9).
Only locate-and-edit methods are studied; other editors are not covered (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Figure 2: Overview of REP. Left: Key concept visualization; Right: Architectural design of the adapter.

novelty_note.C: Whitened-space similarity under ROME's covariance inverse decides which keys match, a covariance-inverse metric rather than a gate or steering direction built from discriminant analysis.
novelty_note.G: Shows key collisions: 'Michael Jordan' and 'Kobe Bryant' overlap in the whitened space, so the similarity signal reflects relatedness rather than the intended fact.

title: WISE: Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of Large Language Models
question: Can lifelong model editing satisfy reliability, generalization and locality together, if edits are stored in a side memory rather than in the main weights or in retrieved activations?
mechanism: A side FFN value matrix W_v' holds the edits while the main W_v stays frozen. A routing indicator Delta_act(x) = ||A(x) (W_v' - W_v)||_2 (Eq. 3), computed from the layer's activation A(x), is trained with a margin loss (Eq. 5) so that edit inputs score above beta and irrelevant inputs below alpha. The threshold epsilon is the smallest edit score seen so far; at inference the side memory is used if Delta_act(x) > epsilon, otherwise the main memory (Eq. 6). Continual edits are split into shards in distinct parameter subspaces and merged into one shared side memory (WISE-Merge) without conflicts (Sec. 2.3).
training: Gradient-based: each shard's side memory is trained with the autoregressive loss plus the routing loss L_a (Sec. 2.3); the main model is not updated. Edit counts go up to T=1000 in Table 2.
inference_cost: Reported: WISE-Merge adds 'constant additional costs (0.64% extra parameters and 4% extra GPU VRAM)'; WISE-Retrieve inference time rises by 'about 7% after 3K edits' (inference-time analysis).
setup: LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B on ZsRE QA, hallucination and out-of-distribution sets, with sequential edits T = 1, 10, 100, 1000; baselines ROME, MEMIT, MEMIT-MASS, FT-EWC, MEND, DEFER and GRACE.
numbers: Table 2 (ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B, T=100): WISE Reliability 0.90, Generalization 0.81, Locality 1.00, Average 0.90; ROME at T=100 Average 0.16.
Table 2 (LLaMA-2-7B, T=1000): WISE Average 0.83 vs GRACE 0.67 and MEMIT-MASS 0.65.
limits: Side-memory retrieval has room for improvement to reach the oracle (Table 6).
WISE-Retrieve's inference time grows with the number of edits (Fig. 6).
Because edits live in a separate side memory, users can discard them without modifying the main LLM (Limitations and Broader Impacts).
evidence_quote: We only edit the knowledge in the side memory and train a router to decide which memory to go through when given a query.

novelty_note.B: The routing indicator Delta_act(x) is computed from the layer's own FFN activation with no separate classifier and selects between two weight branches per input; it routes a trained weight edit rather than a steering vector.

title: $μ$KE: Matryoshka Unstructured Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
question: Does unstructured (long-form) knowledge editing with window-by-window updates break dependencies between early memory edits and later output tokens, and can a Matryoshka objective fix it?
mechanism: Locate-and-edit computes working-memory updates delta_i at selected layers for each window, then maps them to weights with constrained optimization. The Matryoshka objective L_mu is a weighted mean in which each working memory is trained against all later target tokens, so gradients flow from later tokens back to earlier memories; adaptive coefficients lambda_{i,j} balance window terms according to the affinity of their gradient directions (Sec. 3.2-3.3).
training: Gradient-based: working memories and weight shifts are optimized with gradient descent; edit batch size 1 and decoding temperature 0.001, following AnyEdit (Sec. 4). No training-data size is extracted.
setup: Two LLMs on five unstructured-editing benchmarks, compared with AnyEdit and locate-and-edit baselines such as MEMIT and AlphaEdit (model names not extracted).
numbers: Abstract: 'µKE improves edit efficacy by up to 12.33% over state-of-the-art methods'.
Results (Table 1): 'up to 12.33% with the original question and 10.5% with the paraphrased question of absolute improvement' in BLEU over AnyEdit.
limits: The locate-and-edit optimization is coupled to fixed learning rates and step counts; adaptive coefficients only partly address this (Limitations).
Existing benchmarks lack annotations of fine-grained knowledge units within long targets, limiting evaluation (Limitations).
evidence_quote: This memory update objective targets a series of condensed representation shifts (partially) covering the corresponding subsequent edit target in the sequential update process.

title: MELO: Enhancing Model Editing with Neuron-Indexed Dynamic LoRA
question: Can model editing satisfy edit success, locality, generality and sequential editing together, with high efficiency, by adding a small LoRA block per edit batch and indexing it in a vector database?
mechanism: Training: each edit batch is learned in a fresh, non-overlapping LoRA block of partial rank p, updated by W_B^t <- W_B^t - eta grad L[f(X_e^t; W_B^t W_A^t), Y_e^t] (Eq. 8-9). Inference: the last hidden state h_l of the input is the key K_q, matched to the nearest cluster centre in a vector database. If K_q falls within that cluster's radius, the LoRA block recorded for the nearest stored key is activated; otherwise no block is applied. Cluster radii expand under explicit rules when an edit falls just outside them (Sec. 3).
training: Gradient descent on LoRA blocks only, per edit batch (learning rates in Table 1: 1e-3 for BERT, T5-Small and T5-Large, 1e-4 for GPT2-XL). No retraining of the base model. Data: SCOTUS, zsRE and a hallucination set.
inference_cost: Not quantified; the paper states MELO 'requires the least trainable parameters and computational cost' among the compared editors.
setup: BERT on SCOTUS (Fairlex), T5-Small and T5-Large on zsRE, GPT2-XL on hallucination correction; baselines LoRA, MEND, SERAC, CMR, ROME, GRACE.
numbers: Table 2, MELO row: '0.96 0.92 0.72 0.98 0.97 17.45 1.04 2.66' (the column grouping is garbled in the text extraction; the table reports locality, edit success, generality and perplexity/ARR metrics).
limits: No limitations section was found in the read text. interp: the radius and cluster rules are hand-set hyperparameters (Table 1).
evidence_quote: Each batch of edits is learned in a set of LoRA blocks located in different layers

novelty_note.B: A nearest-neighbour lookup on the last hidden state with no separate classifier decides which LoRA block to apply; the gated object is a trained low-rank block rather than a steering vector.

title: ORBIT: Training-Free Multi-Attribute Behavioral Steering via Orthogonal Subspace Rotation
question: How can several behavioural attributes be steered at once without training, when summed steering vectors cancel and dominate each other?
mechanism: Per attribute k: a 2D plane (b1 = contrastive mean direction, b2 = first PCA direction of paired differences, orthogonalized against b1). Signed projection s_k = h . b1_hat and zero-margin gate g_k = max(0, -s_k) (Eq. 2-3), so aligned tokens are untouched. Gate-weighted aggregate target r = sum_k g_k b1_hat (Eq. 4). Planes are merged by SVD into one orthonormal joint subspace, and the in-subspace component is rotated norm-preservingly toward the target while the orthogonal component is unchanged. An optional additive boost is scaled by the same gates (Eq. 9).
training: None: training-free, using contrastive activation pairs to form each attribute's direction; no classifier training. Joint success rates are in Appendix F.1.
setup: Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; TraitFactory (13 traits, 20 topics) and ToneBank (5 tones); GPT-4o-mini judge (0-10) and a coherence score; baselines CAA, K-Steering, MAT-STEER and MSRS.
numbers: Table 1, ToneBank, Llama-3.2-3B, K=2: unsteered judge 5.06 (coherence 90.8); CAA 5.72 / 86.2 with geometric gain +0.44; K-Steer 4.91 / 83.8 with -0.12; ORBIT 5.94 / 88.0 with +0.81.
limits: Relies on approximately linear attribute representations; attributes with nonlinear or entangled representations may not be captured by one direction (Sec. 9).
Suppression of attributes is demonstrated only in a limited setting; a systematic study of mitigating multiple undesirable behaviours is left to future work (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Continuous gates from signed projections determine pass-through, single-trait, or joint steering

novelty_note.B: The gate g_k = max(0, -s_k) is a signed projection of the hidden state onto each attribute axis, with no separate classifier, and it decides per token whether and how much to steer.
novelty_note.E: Section 3.4 characterizes geometric failure modes of naive additive steering (norm dominance and pairwise angular conflict), and the introduction argues that the chance of pairs with substantial negative cosine similarity rises as attributes are added.

title: ARM: Role-Conditioned Neuron Transplantation for Training-Free Generalist LLM Agent Merging
question: Can a training-free merge of agent experts keep role-critical behaviour, such as tool-call formatting, by selecting a backbone and transplanting role-salient MLP neurons?
mechanism: Role-conditioned saliency s_{l,j}(M; b, r) is the expected per-role mean MLP activation over calibration trajectories (Eq. 2). Backbone selection uses an Activation-Overlap Score: the overlap between the candidate backbone's top-k% role-salient neurons and the expert's, per benchmark. Neuron transplantation copies a small top-k% set of donor MLP neurons from the expert into the chosen backbone, protecting neurons salient for other benchmarks.
training: None: the abstract states that 'without gradient-based optimization' ARM improves cross-benchmark generalization. A calibration set is used for activation tracing.
setup: Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B expert pools on WebShop, OfficeBench, tau-bench, OS and other agent suites, plus out-of-domain benchmarks; baselines Task Arithmetic, TIES and Model Stock.
numbers: Sec. 4: 'the overlap rate drops from 61% to 41% on Qwen3-8B, and from 50% to 43% on Qwen2.5-7B' with role-conditioned tracing versus role-agnostic tracing.
limits: Requires homologous expert checkpoints with the same architecture and tokenizer; does not apply to heterogeneous families or black-box APIs (Sec. 6).
Activation-level diagnostics for multi-turn agent behaviour remain under-explored (Sec. 6).
evidence_quote: Without gradient-based optimization, ARM improves cross-benchmark generalization while enjoying efficiency.

title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
question: Where are abilities stored in LLM parameters, and can an ability be transferred or recovered by moving only the parameters of activation-selected channels?
mechanism: Channel identification: feed the same inputs to the ability model and the base model, average activations over answer tokens per output channel, and rank channels by the activation difference Delta a_i; the top p% form an ability mask M_act. Masks from several ability models are aggregated into one unified mask. The task vector Delta theta = theta_abl - theta_trg (task arithmetic) is applied only to the rows the mask selects, followed by a lightweight fine-tuning step (Sec. 4.1-4.3).
training: Activations and masks come from forward passes. Post-transfer fine-tuning is gradient-based, on the same ability datasets (about 1500 instances per ability in the text read). No training-cost totals are extracted.
setup: A Qwen2.5-Math-7B model pair for multilingual mathematics (MetaMathQA translations) and science (MegaScience translations, 11 languages); compared with task arithmetic, TIES and DARE.
numbers: Abstract: 'ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5%)'.
Table 1: overlap of top-1% activation-difference channels across abilities for Qwen2.5-7B Math-Instruct vs. Instruct (values not extracted).
limits: No limitations section was found in the read text (interp: results are reported on one model pair).
Post-transfer fine-tuning improves compatibility, so the transfer alone is not sufficient for the best reported scores (Sec. 4.3).
evidence_quote: select the top p% to form an activation-based ability-specific mask

title: Probe-Free Low-Rank Activation Intervention
question: Can an activation intervention that needs no probe improve truthfulness, by pushing activations of one layer toward the region of desirable answers?
mechanism: FLORAIN models desirable answers for each question as an ellipsoid with centre mu_q, a shared covariance Sigma^-1 (an LDA-style assumption) and radius rho_q; under Mahalanobis distance the projection onto the ellipsoid has an analytical form (Thm. 4.1). The intervention in the heads of one layer is a sample-wise nonlinear low-rank map; its parameters minimize the distance between the modified activations and the projection, with alpha weighting local (question-specific) against global (overall) directions. Training uses scaled gradient descent with the inverse covariance as preconditioner (Sec. 4).
training: Gradient-based: parameters of the low-rank map are fit by (preconditioned) gradient descent on activations of desirable and undesirable TruthfulQA answers. Sample sizes are not extracted; the paper notes the ellipsoid estimate is sensitive to small training sets (Limitations).
inference_cost: Claimed, not measured: intervening in one layer 'provides conditions for parallelization to reduce inference intervention time' (Sec. 1).
setup: Llama-7B, Llama3-8B and Llama2-chat-13B on TruthfulQA (generation and multiple-choice), and Alpaca and Vicuna on instruction-tuned tasks; baseline ITI.
numbers: Table 1, Llama-7B: unintervened True*Info 21.15; ITI 26.52; FLORAIN 31.46 (True 34.72, MC1 31.76, MC2 47.43, CE 2.21, KL 0.09).
limits: Depends on the scale of the training dataset; with few samples the mean and covariance estimates are biased (Limitations).
The optimization is nonconvex and the first-order algorithm may converge to local minimizers (Limitations).
evidence_quote: we propose to use preconditioned gradient descent, the scaled convex combination

novelty_note.C: The projection uses a Mahalanobis distance with a shared inverse covariance Sigma^-1, as in linear discriminant analysis, to define the target region for steering.

title: On Task Vectors and Gradients
question: Why does task arithmetic work, and when is merging single-epoch task vectors as good as merging converged ones?
mechanism: Full-batch GD with step eta on task t: the one-epoch task vector tau_t = theta_t^(1) - theta_base = -eta grad L_t(theta_base), so the sum of task vectors equals one GD step on the summed multitask loss with effective step alpha*eta. For k>1 epochs the deviation from joint training is a second-order term O(eta^2), with explicit 2-norm bounds for feed-forward networks that assume bounded weights and activations with bounded derivatives (Sec. 2-3).
training: Gradient-based fine-tuning of vision models on seven benchmarks; the analysis is of full-batch GD and the paper gives no training-cost totals.
setup: Seven vision benchmarks (including SVHN and DTD) with task arithmetic and merging of one-epoch versus converged fine-tuned models.
numbers: Sec. 2.1: the gradients from the first 5 epochs maintain a high cosine similarity (> 0.8) with the first epoch's gradient (Fig. 3b).
limits: The theory is for full-batch GD, while the empirical setting uses SGD-style finetuning (Sec. 2).
The multi-epoch error bound is second order and depends on the stated boundedness assumptions (Sec. 2-3).
evidence_quote: We show that under standard gradient descent, a task vector generated from one epoch of finetuning is exactly equivalent to the negative gradient of the loss, scaled by the learning rate.
